https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0n.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach it By Laura Gozzi Â and Â Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Published 30 July 2026 Hungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar has said. The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it. Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week. Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer. The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania. Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment. A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Large areas of the riverbed have been exposed in the centre of Budapest after weeks of extreme heat and drought In Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power. The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production. Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe. It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Among the wrecks exposed by the low levels of the Danube was a World War Two German warship at Prahovo in Serbia Romania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second (m3/s) in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600 m3/s. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500 m3/s by Tuesday. The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries. The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea. The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia. And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth. They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib. Image source, Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik/Reuters Image caption, River flow in Serbia on the Danube is now a third of the average for July Shipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania. There were reports of passengers running low of food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, but Viking later told the BBC that "sufficient water remained available for all guests and crew throughout the incident. At no point did the vessel run out of provisions or experience a shortage". "I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Boats lie on the dried-out Danube riverbed in front of the Calafat-Vidin bridge, connecting Bulgaria and Romania It is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube. Serbian hydrologist Dejan VladikoviÄ said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring. He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September. Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C. Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected. Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory , leading to hundreds of thocusands of evacuations. Correction 1 August: This article originally stated that food and water had been running low for passengers on the grounded Viking Ullur and another boat was unable to get close enough with provisions. It was later amended with the company's denial of any shortage. Photograph: Yan Dobronosov/Reuters Opinion Ukraine Russia is raining death on Ukraine’s women and children. Our hands shake, but we keep going for love Alina Sarnatska Our skin has thickened into armour, but I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards others – or myself Wed 9 Sep 2026 00.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.17 EDT Share M y grandma was as hard as nails. She had just turned 17 when the Nazis entered her village in the Kyiv region, near what is now the city of Bucha. She hid in the attic to avoid being taken for forced labour. They didn’t find her that time, but a few weeks later she was caught working in the fields. They put her in a cattle wagon and took her to Germany. She escaped and walked a couple of hundred kilometres back to her village. Grandma said that life was hard for everybody during the war, but she was lucky. In the past month, two of my friends here in Kyiv happened to tell me that their hands have started shaking during Russian airstrikes. Everybody who knows that my hands shake during airstrikes tells me their stories. One day, during an airstrike in the Donetsk region, I had a meltdown and have never recovered. Today you could say I am an ambassador for people whose hands shake during airstrikes. Those two friends said the same exact thing: their hands never used to shake before and now they do. Each one wrote: “I don’t understand what’s just happened to me.” For nearly five years, the Russians have been targeting these women and their children with drones, rockets, jet-powered drones and missiles. They have threatened us with nuclear weapons. They have used an Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile in combat; carried out a siege ; again threatened a nuclear strike; tried to freeze us by destroying Ukraine’s heat and power systems in the middle of winter; blown up a dam , flooding two city districts; used more drones and fired yet other types of long-range missiles at Ukrainian cities; organised terror attacks ; and, once again, threatened to wipe us out with nuclear weapons. In the early hours of 19 July, the general staff of the armed forces of Ukraine reported a massive combined Russian attack : 41 missiles and 125 drones, with Kyiv as the main target. Next morning, I got a message from my friend Valya. “Everything was fine, and then all of a sudden something happened,” she wrote. “Everyone but me is at home asleep. I’m the only one who’s so anxious.” After every airstrike, the women I know “pull themselves together”, take their children to preschool, and go to work. Because children need to be fed – and if the state-run preschool doesn’t have a bomb shelter, the private one that does costs money. The women I know sleep beside their children in the corridors of their apartment buildings, in underground parking garages, in the metro or in pedestrian tunnels. “Everything’s fine,” say these women. After Russia fires dozens of missiles at Kyiv overnight, they say: “It was loud, but everything’s fine.” And they wonder why their hands shake and they even blame themselves for being weak. View image in fullscreen Russian missile strike in Kyiv, 8 September 2026. Photograph: Reuters My grandma’s name was Dina and she was as hard as nails. She would get very angry when I snuggled up to our relatives. Once, my grandma’s sister was over and I climbed on to her lap and wrapped my arms around her. Grandma Dina yelled at me: “Get down, what a disgrace, you’re a big girl now!” I was seven. My grandma was afraid I would be spoiled. Whenever I cried, she would say to my mother: “Look how you’ve spoiled her, how will she cope with life?” Grandma Dina liked to feed stray cats. Grandpa protested, but she did it anyway. When she went out to feed them, for a few minutes she became a completely different person. First, she scolded them for being a nuisance, wearing her usual face. Then, as they ate, she would start to smile a bit and stroke their thin, fluffy backs. With one hand on her thigh, she would lean over and pet each cat once or twice, smiling. Then she would pick up the bowl, straighten up, and her expression would return to normal. One morning, I found a large grey cat dead under a bush; a cat that my grandma had been feeding for 10 years, as long as I had been alive. He had probably died of old age or sickness. I burst into tears and ran to my grandma. She rolled up a towel and gave me a whack on the ribs. “Now stop that crying, you’re a big girl now!” When my mother came home from work in the evening, I said: “I think Grandma’s a robot.” To which mum replied: “Nonsense, now go finish your soup.” There was nothing soft about Grandma Dina. If she were still alive today, she would be well prepared. She didn’t know much about getting along with people, but she did know how to pull herself together. Now I understand that she could not cut herself any slack or allow herself any feelings of self-kindness and that’s why she also felt no compassion for others. Compassion was too risky for her. And it’s true, we cannot let ourselves be as emotional or compassionate as we were before the war. We cannot live, let alone work, as we did before. On top of that, war reveals the sharp contrast between our reality and the cult of the self displayed on social media. Viral posts about “success, energy and choosing yourself” are irrelevant to anyone caring for a sick child when it is 5C inside your apartment. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Enduring daily death and the violence of Russia’s attacks has changed us irreversibly. The skin of Ukrainian women has thickened into armour. These women take part in combat, live under constant airstrikes, and keep working and caring for their families through it all. But if it were up to me, I would keep my belly soft. I still want to hug people, hold them close, and feel the warmth of their hands. So what if Grandma Dina would say I’m not ready for life? I think that love is worth the risk. We stay calm because our children are watching us, because they need to be taken to preschool in the morning, because there is still work to do. But when resilience becomes an obligation, every trembling hand starts to feel like a personal failure. I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards other people, or towards myself. Translated from Ukrainian by Larissa Babij Alina Sarnatska is a Ukrainian writer, playwright and war veteran. She is the author of two books and nine plays, and her work has been staged and presented internationally Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Reuters Universities Analysis MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.36 EDT First published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.07 EDT Share The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival. The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”. The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency. MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research Read more China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work. This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers. Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert , warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence. Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act , which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities. The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy. Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector. There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”. In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography , the embedding of hidden data in pictures online. Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics. “It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said. Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields. Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.” The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes. That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades. Exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania, and borders ‌the Baltic Sea Burc Eruygur 05 October 2026 • Update : 05 October 2026 ISTANBUL Russia said could use 'all weapons' in arsenal in case of direct attack on region; NATO dismissed warnings, urging to 'stop the nuclear threats' Russia’s westernmost Kaliningrad region has recently become a focal point of tensions with the West, as Russia threatened to use "all weapons" in its arsenal to defend the territory. At a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow last week, President Vladimir Putin said any direct attack on Russia or attempt to annex the exclave would inevitably raise the issue of using "all weapons and means at Moscow’s disposal." Noting that a Foreign Ministry letter on the protection of the Kaliningrad region does not mention nuclear weapons, Putin said the memo was issued in response to statements about a possible blockade of the exclave, and that Russia would have to respond if the region faced a direct attack. A number of Russian embassies in Europe, including Ireland and the UK, also commented on “provocative” statements concerning Kaliningrad's blockade. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte did not disclose what was in the letter, but said the organization responded that "we are a defensive alliance," calling on Russia to "stop the nuclear threats" and "stop the war in Ukraine." Russia’s sole exclave With a population of about 1 million, the Kaliningrad region is a semi-exclave bordering Lithuania to the north and east, Poland to the south, and the Baltic Sea to the west. It is separated from Belarus, a close ally of Russia with which it is formally part of a union state since 1999, by a roughly 65-kilometer (40.3-mile) corridor at its shortest point, known as the Suwalki Gap. Named after the nearby Polish town of Suwalki, the gap serves as NATO’s only land route to the Baltic states and has gained particular geopolitical importance following Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania’s accession to the alliance in March 2004. All three Baltic states also joined the EU later that year. The regional capital of Kaliningrad, a major port city on the Baltic coast that served as a former capital of the Kingdom of Prussia under the name of Konigsberg, became part of the Soviet Union after the end of World War II. It was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946 in honor of Mikhail Kalinin, a Soviet politician who served as a chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet between 1938 and 1946. The city is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet. From here, Russia oversees large swaths of the Baltic’s airspace and maritime territory, but in the event of a war, it could struggle to sustain its forces if communications were disrupted. Why the latest tensions? Tensions have continued since the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022, leading to NATO strengthening its eastern flank. Finland and Sweden, which have a coast to the Baltic Sea, also joined the alliance in 2023 and 2024, ​respectively. The latest spike came after NATO conducted a planned yet unannounced air exercise above northeastern Poland near the Kaliningrad region in August. The operation is said to have demonstrated the capability to cut off the exclave's radio and radar links as well as its air defenses in the event of a conflict with Russia. The flights came after German newspaper Bild reported that the alliance developed the Land Warfighting Concept for responding to a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states, including strikes on missile and air defense systems in the region. In May, Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said NATO has the means to destroy air defense capabilities in Kaliningrad. "We must show the Russians that we are capable of breaking through their little fortress in Kaliningrad. If necessary, NATO has all the means to level the Russian air defense and missile bases there," Budrys said in an interview with the Swiss Neue Zurcher Zeitung newspaper.
